## The question

[mean Value Integral](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2069994/mean-value-integral), asked by [Numerical Person](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/173803/numerical-person) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-12-23; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
> I can solve this integral in the very general way. But I don't unnderstand  how they have applied the mean value theorem to this integral and solve this? 
>
>
>   [q-1]: tiI8p.png
:::

The **Integral Mean Value Theorem** says that if $f$ is integrable on $[A,B]$, then 
$$\int_A^B f(x)\,dx = (B-A) f(c)$$
for some $c$ in $(A,B)$.

In your first integral you have $A = \frac{L}{4} - \frac{a}{2}$ and $B = \frac{L}{4} + \frac{a}{2}$.  So $B- A = a$, and since $a$ is “small enough” (according to the note), $c \approx \frac{L}{4}$.  Hence
$$\int_{L/4 - a/2}^{L/4 + a/2} f(x)\,dx \approx a f\left(\frac{L}{4}\right)$$
The other integral is treated similarly.
